title: Area II review: Preflight Procedures
intro: These questions mix all three Tasks of Area II: aircraft systems, flight instruments and navigation equipment, and the instrument flight deck check. Many join two Tasks in one real IFR preflight or flight, just like the checkride.

questions.q: You departed with the altimeter set to 30.12. An hour later you are cruising at 7,000 ft indicated and have not reset it. The local altimeter setting is now 29.82. About what is your true altitude?
questions.why: A change of 1 inch on the barometric scale moves the altimeter 1,000 ft [[23:99|IFH 5-4]]. 30.12 - 29.82 = 0.30 inch, about 300 ft. Flying into lower pressure without resetting puts you lower than indicated: "from a high to a low, look out below" [[23:102|IFH 5-7]]. So 7,000 - 300 = about 6,700 ft.

questions.q: Your airplane has a fluid ice protection system (fluid weeps out of the wing leading edges). During the IFH instrument check, what do you check before engine start, and what after?
options: Before start: that it works properly. After start: the fluid quantity left.
Before start: availability and fluid quantity. After start: that it works.
Only the fluid quantity before start. Its operation is checked later, in cloud.
Nothing before start. The run-up checks both the quantity and the flow of fluid.
questions.why: Before engine start, check the deicing and anti-icing equipment for availability and fluid quantity. After engine start, check its operation [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

questions.q: On preflight, the attitude indicator in your piston single (no MEL) will not erect. You planned to fly IFR. What is true under 14 CFR 91.213(d)?
options: You may defer it if you placard it INOP and decide it is not a hazard
It can't be deferred for IFR, because 91.205(d) requires it for IFR flight
You may defer it if a mechanic makes a logbook entry for it first
You may defer it if the turn coordinator and heading indicator both work
questions.why: 91.213(d) does not let you defer equipment required by 91.205 for the kind of flight you are making [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. For IFR, 91.205(d) requires a gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)]]. Placarding and a pilot's hazard decision only apply to equipment that passes those tests first [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]].

questions.q: ATC offers you a vector to join the RNAV (GPS) final course 1 NM outside the final approach waypoint (FAWP). Why does the AIM recommend against accepting it?
options: The GPS can't arm the approach mode any closer than 5 NM from the FAWP, so it flags
The CDI goes back to en route sensitivity of 5 NM in that area until you pass the FAWP
RAIM switches off inside 2 NM of the FAWP and stays off until you pass the waypoint
The CDI scale tightens there, so a good intercept can look like drifting off
questions.why: Starting 2 NM before the FAWP, full-scale CDI sensitivity smoothly changes from 1 NM to 0.3 NM. If you are not yet centered, the growing needle deflection can look like you are moving away, even on a good intercept heading. So the AIM says requesting or accepting vectors that join final within 2 NM of the FAWP is not recommended [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]].

questions.q: You plan an IFR flight in an airplane not approved for flight in icing. The destination METAR shows ice pellets at the surface and a temperature of -1 °C. What may this observation mean?
options: Ice pellets don't stick to the airplane, so ice is not a concern on the approach
The whole column of air aloft is below freezing, so only dry snow is likely aloft
Freezing drizzle or freezing rain (large drops) may be present aloft
Only light rime is likely in the clouds, and the pitot heat will handle all of it
questions.why: Ice pellets do not ice the airframe themselves, but seen on the ground they can mean supercooled large drops aloft [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1l]], possibly freezing drizzle or freezing rain [[38:60|AC 91-74B App 2]]. In an airplane not certified for icing, plan to avoid it and have an escape plan [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1m]].

questions.q: Before taxi for an IFR flight, the VSI shows a steady 100 fpm climb. Tapping the panel does not change it, and the static ports are clear. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Cancel IFR, because the VSI is required for IFR
Open the alternate static source to zero the needle
Use the 100 fpm reading as your zero mark and fly
Set the altimeter 100 ft lower to cancel the error
questions.why: The IFH check is a zero reading, tapping the panel if it is off [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. If the VSI still shows something other than zero, that reading can be used as the zero mark [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]. A VSI is not on the 91.205(d) list of IFR equipment [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]].

questions.q: In your glass-panel airplane the alternator failed, the main battery ran down, and the standby battery came online. According to the IFH, what does the essential bus usually power?
options: AHRS, air data computer, PFD, NAV 1 and COM 1
The MFD moving map, autopilot, COM 2 and landing light
Only the standby attitude indicator, altimeter and compass
Both GPS navigators, the PFD and the MFD
questions.why: With its switch in ARM, the standby battery comes online near 19 volts and powers the essential bus: usually the AHRS, ADC, PFD, NAV 1, COM 1 and the standby indicator light [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. The standby attitude indicator, altimeter, airspeed indicator and compass are there for when the PFD is not available [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

questions.q: Your ETA at the destination is 1440. You ask flight service for GPS RAIM information and don't name a time period. What period will the briefer give you?
questions.why: Unless you ask for a specific period, FAA briefers give RAIM information from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA hour [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(2)]]. The ETA hour is 1400 to 1500, so you get 1300 to 1600. The AIM example works the same way: a 1215 arrival gives 1100 to 1400 [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(2)]].

questions.q: On the walk-around before an IFR flight in rain, you find two static wicks broken off the trailing edges. What does the IFH say?
options: They are cosmetic; P-static only causes harmless St. Elmo's fire on the windshield
Go, but keep the pitot heat off and fly low to reduce the build-up of static charge
They only matter for the ADF receiver, so you may go as long as you don't use it
Replace them first; P-static can cause loss of VHF comm and compass errors
questions.why: Broken or missing static wicks should be replaced before an instrument flight [[23:328|IFH 11-3]]. Precipitation static, usually met in rain or snow, can cause erroneous magnetic compass readings and even complete loss of VHF communications [[23:328|IFH 11-3]]. Static wicks are on the list of items to check closely before IFR [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].

questions.q: You climb through cloud at OAT -4 °C and forgot to turn on the pitot heat. At constant pitch and power, the airspeed now rises as you climb, and it falls when you descend a little. What is the most likely cause?
options: Ice blocked both the pitot ram hole and its drain hole
Ice blocked only the pitot ram hole; the drain is open
Airframe ice is building, so the airplane is losing lift
Ice blocked the static ports, so the airspeed is frozen
questions.why: If the ram hole and the drain hole are both blocked, the airspeed indicator works like an altimeter as you climb and descend. With only the ram hole blocked and the drain open, it slowly drops to zero instead [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. Even light icing can block the pitot entry hole, which is why pitot heat is fitted [[38:28|AC 91-74B 3-11a]]. Turn it on.

questions.q: Your 3,400 lb single was certified for flight in icing in 1985. Ice remains on the airframe as you fly the ILS to a long runway. The AFM has no flap limits for icing. What landing does AC 91-74B suggest you consider?
options: Full flaps, adding 10 knots to the normal approach speed
Full flaps, to keep the approach speed and landing roll as low as possible
A partial-flap or no-flap landing, with a faster approach and longer roll
Normal flaps and speed, because the airplane is certified for icing
questions.why: If the airplane was certified for icing before 1994 and weighs under 19,000 lb, consider a partial- or no-flap landing [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10e(2)]]. Tailplane stall rarely happens until the flaps are fully extended [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10e]]. Without an AFM icing speed, increase approach speed at least 25 percent and expect a longer landing distance [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10f]].

questions.q: Your airplane's altimeter and altitude reporting system were tested 8 months ago, up to a maximum altitude of 12,000 ft. On an IFR flight in controlled airspace, ATC offers 14,000 ft to top a cloud layer. What is true?
options: You must decline; you can't fly IFR there above the tested altitude
You may accept, but you must turn off altitude reporting above 12,000 ft
You may accept, because the 24-month test is still current after only 8 months
You may accept if you carry supplemental oxygen for the climb above 12,500 ft
questions.why: No one may fly an airplane under IFR in controlled airspace above the maximum altitude to which all its altimeters and its altitude reporting system have been tested [[60:525|14 CFR 91.411(d)]]. A current 24-month test [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(1)]] does not raise that limit.

questions.q: In IMC, your left display goes black and the system switches as shown in the bottom picture. What is now true?
options: The other screen keeps the full moving map, and you fly on the standby gauges alone
The other screen shows the flight instruments and engine data, but no full map
Both screens show only engine data until you pull and reset the AHRS circuit breaker
The flight data moves to the standby instruments only, and the MFD goes completely blank
questions.why: When a display fails, the system goes to a composite (reversionary) mode. It combines the PFD with the engine indicating system and eliminates the moving map display [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].

questions.q: On the before-start check for an IFR flight, how does the IFH suggest you check the pitot heat?
options: Turn it on in the run-up and watch the airspeed needle rise
Watch the ammeter as you turn it on, or use the POH method
Leave it on for 10 minutes on the ramp, then grip the tube
There is no ground check; you confirm it in visible moisture
questions.why: The IFH before-start list says: check the pitot tube heater by watching the ammeter when it is turned on, or by using the method in the POH/AFM [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. The pitot heater is electric, so a working heater shows up as an electrical load [[23:97|IFH 5-2]].

questions.q: You fly a fuel-injected single with a constant-speed prop in freezing cloud and wet snow. Manifold pressure slowly drops while rpm stays steady. What is likely, and what do you do?
options: Impact ice is blocking the air intake; select alternate air
The vacuum pump is failing; check the suction gauge and the gyro flags
Ice is building on the propeller; increase rpm to throw the ice off
Carburetor ice is forming in the induction system; apply full carburetor heat
questions.why: Ice on the normal induction air source shows as a loss of manifold pressure with a constant-speed prop, or a loss of rpm with a fixed-pitch prop. A fuel-injected engine has no carburetor, so select alternate air; on some engines it opens automatically [[24:258|AFH 13-9]].

questions.q: Your only IFR navigator is a TSO-C129 GPS with no WAAS. On the run-up, the VOR receiver fails and you have no other VOR or DME. Your route is all GPS airways. May you depart IFR on the GPS alone?
options: Yes, because the GPS is IFR approved and RAIM is predicted for the whole route
Yes, as long as you tell ATC about the VOR failure and change the equipment suffix
No, unless flight service gives you a RAIM prediction for the whole route first
No; un-augmented GPS needs another approved, working means of navigation
questions.why: Aircraft using un-augmented GPS (TSO-C129) under IFR must have an alternate approved and operational means of navigation for the route, such as VOR. RAIM only means you don't have to actively monitor that backup; it does not replace having it [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(a)(2)]].

questions.q: Your heading indicator has failed, and ATC asks you to fly magnetic heading 300. The radios are on. Using this compass correction card, what compass heading should you hold?
questions.why: The card gives the compass heading to steer for each magnetic heading. For 300 with the radios on it says steer 296; 298 is the radios-off value [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]. The IFH example reads it the same way: for 120 with radios on, fly 123 [[23:108|IFH 5-13]].

questions.q: You pick up light rime in cloud, and ATC assigns a hold at 5,000 ft. To slow down, you think about holding with partial flaps. What does AC 91-74B advise?
options: Holding is safer than cruise in ice, because power is lower and the speed is slower
Expect more ice in the hold, and check the AFM, which may ban flaps in ice
Engage the autopilot and slow to just above the stall warning to cut ice collection
Use full flaps, because a slower speed lowers the ice collection rate in the hold
questions.why: An airplane may be more vulnerable to ice in a hold because of the slower speeds and lower altitudes [[38:50|AC 91-74B 5-9a]]. Consult the AFM for flap use; many AFMs prohibit flaps for extended periods in icing conditions [[38:50|AC 91-74B 5-9d]]. If the airplane reacts badly to a configuration change, return to the original configuration [[38:50|AC 91-74B 5-9c]].

questions.q: On the arrival, you load the RNAV approach and compare it with the chart. One waypoint name in the navigator is spelled differently from the chart. What does the AIM say?
options: Enter the chart's waypoint by hand and fly the approach that way
Use it; small spelling differences between box and chart are normal
Use it if the waypoint sits in the right place on the map
Don't use that waypoint; names must exactly match the chart
questions.why: In flight, check that waypoint and transition names match the chart, and don't use waypoints that don't exactly match the spelling on the published chart [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(4)]]. You may never build an approach by entering waypoints by hand [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(3)]].

questions.q: The shop installed a new transponder last week. Your 24-month altimeter, static and encoder checks were done 5 months ago. Before IFR in controlled airspace, what else is needed?
options: Nothing; the 24-month checks done 5 months ago still cover the new transponder
Nothing; a newly installed transponder starts its own fresh 24-month period
Only a radio check with ATC to confirm that your Mode C readout looks right
A test of the integrated system for altitude data correspondence
questions.why: After installation or maintenance on a transponder where data correspondence error could be introduced, the integrated system must be tested and inspected to paragraph (c) of part 43 appendix E [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(b)]] [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(3)]]. As installed, the reported altitude must match the altimeter within 125 ft [[60:495|14 CFR 91.217(a)(2)]].

questions.q: Your MFD moving map works well. Why does the IFH still tell you to follow the flight on the en route chart?
options: The en route chart is the only source ATC accepts for your position reports in IFR
The map is a supplementary source; if a screen fails, you lose your position
The rules require a current paper chart open in front of you during every IFR flight
The moving map is not accurate enough to show airways and fixes in a reliable way
questions.why: The electronic flight display is a supplementary source of navigation data and does not replace en route charts. Follow the flight on the chart and know the closest airport, because that becomes critical if the display fails [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].

questions.q: You fly Part 91 with a tablet EFB instead of paper charts. Your chart subscription lapsed, and the app still shows last cycle's approach charts. What does AC 91-78A say?
options: They're fine, because Part 91 EFB use needs no FAA approval
They're fine, as long as you also carry a backup tablet
Not usable in place of paper; the data must be current and valid
Usable for en route only, because airways rarely change
questions.why: An EFB may replace paper only when the information used for navigation or performance planning is current, up to date and valid, as verified by the pilot [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]]. Part 91 in-flight EFB use needs no formal approval, but only when the AC's guidelines are followed [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.2]].

questions.q: You are departing from a small field with no weather reporting, and you can't get a current altimeter setting before takeoff. How does the IFH say to set the altimeter for the preflight check?
options: Set it to the published field elevation
Set 29.92 and correct it once airborne
Use the setting from your last flight
Skip the check until you get a setting
questions.why: When no altimeter setting is available, set the altimeter to the published field elevation during the preflight instrument check [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. With a current setting, it should read within 75 ft of field elevation [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].
